# Theme ------------------------------------------------------------------------

  theme_bw() +
    theme(

# Toy data ---------------------------------------------------------------------
y <- c(6.1, 5.4, 7.2, 8.9, 9.1, 11.6)
x1 <- c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3)
x2 <- c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1)

toy_data <- tibble(y, x1, x2)

small_data <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(2, 3, 5))

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, we should be able to:

- Read and write a regression model in matrix form,
  **and explain what each piece means**.
- Explain what the OLS estimator is *trying to do* before you see the formula.
- Derive the normal equations geometrically (no calculus needed) and with
  calculus.
- Estimate the error variance and the coefficient covariance matrix.
- Construct confidence and prediction intervals.
- Reproduce all of the above in R.

## The big picture

We already know how to fit a regression model

Today, we will express the same ideas using matrices

$$
\boxed{
\text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Predictions} \rightarrow \text{Residuals} \rightarrow \text{Minimise SSE}
}
$$

Matrix notation lets us perform these calculations for many observations
and many predictors at once

## Why use matrix notation

Let's suppose we have $n$ observations and $k$ predictors

For each observation we can write

$$
Y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ik} + \varepsilon_i
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Writing this equation separately **for every observation** becomes tedious

Matrix notation allows us to represent all $n$ equations simultaneously

It also makes the mathematics easier to generalise to more complicated
linear models

:::

## Why use matrix notation

### A small example

Suppose we have three observations and two predictors

$$
\begin{align*}
Y_1 &= \beta_0+\beta_1X_{11}+\beta_2X_{12}+\varepsilon_1,\\
Y_2 &= \beta_0+\beta_1X_{21}+\beta_2X_{22}+\varepsilon_2,\\
Y_3 &= \beta_0+\beta_1X_{31}+\beta_2X_{32}+\varepsilon_3
\end{align*}
$$

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Notice that the coefficients **are the same** across observations
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
While the predictor values and errors **vary**
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
How could we **collect these equations** into a single expression?
:::

## Matrix notation

### The response vector

Let $\mathbf Y$ denote the [response vector]{.alert}
(i.e., a vector of observed responses)

$$
\mathbf{Y} = \begin{bmatrix}
Y_1 \\
Y_2 \\
\vdots \\
Y_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

With dimension $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}$

Within this matrix there is one row for every observation and one
column containing the response.

## Matrix notation

### The design matrix

Let $\mathbf{X}$ denote the [design matrix]{.alert} such that:

$$
\mathbf{X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & X_{11} & \cdots &X_{1k} \\
1 & X_{21} & \cdots &X_{2k} \\
\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\
1 & X_{n1} & \cdots & X_{nk}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The first column contains ones because the model includes an intercept

There are $n$ rows and $p = k + 1$ columns such that $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$

Each row represents an observation and each column represents a model term.

## Matrix notation

### The parameter and error vectors

We can collect all the unknown parameters and errors into a
[parameter vector]{.alert} and an [error vector]{.alert}, respectively

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1 \\
\vdots \\
\beta_k
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \begin{bmatrix}
\varepsilon_1 \\
\varepsilon_2 \\
\vdots \\
\varepsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

::::

- Parameter contains $p = k + 1$ parameters
- Error vector contains $n \times 1$ parameters

## Matrix notation {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### The matrix model

In matrix form, the multiple linear regression model thus becomes

$$
\boxed{\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}
$$


$$
\mathbf{Y} = \begin{bmatrix}
Y_1 \\
Y_2 \\
\vdots \\
Y_n
\end{bmatrix} \quad
\mathbf{X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & X_{11} & \cdots &X_{1k} \\
1 & X_{21} & \cdots &X_{2k} \\
\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\
1 & X_{n1} & \cdots & X_{nk}
\end{bmatrix} \quad
\boldsymbol{\beta} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1 \\
\vdots \\
\beta_k
\end{bmatrix} \quad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \begin{bmatrix}
\varepsilon_1 \\
\varepsilon_2 \\
\vdots \\
\varepsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$



:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
where

$$
\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
$$


::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Our objective is to find the coefficient vector that makes these residuals
collectively as small as possible in <br> the least-squares sense.
:::
::::

## Ordinary least squares

Using ordinary least squares we want to minimise

$$
S(\beta) = \sum^n_{j = 1}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_{i1} - \dots - \beta_kx_{ik})^2
$$

In matrix form we can represent this as

$$
S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = (\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why does this work?

- $(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})$ is a **column vector** $(n \times 1)$
- Transposing it turns it into a **row vector** $(1 \times n)$
- We can now calculate the sum of all squared residuals

:::

## Ordinary least squares

If we expand out our above equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) &= (\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta})^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}) \\[4pt]
&=\mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} -\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} \\[4pt]
&=\mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - \underbrace{\mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} -\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y}}_{\text{These two equations are the same}} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} \\[4pt]
&= \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - 2 \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} +\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) =  \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - 2 \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} +\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}}
$$

::: {.notes}
- This is simply a matrix version of $(a - b)(a - b) = a^2 - 2ab + b^2$
:::

## Differentiate to minimise {style="font-size: 80%"}

$$
\boxed{S(\boldsymbol{\beta}) =  \mathbf{Y}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} - 2 \boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} +\boldsymbol{\beta}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}}
$$

When we differentiate the above equation with respect to $\beta$, we are left
with

$$
\frac{\partial S}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} = -2\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} + 2 \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}
$$

Setting this equal to 0

$$
-2 \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{Y} + 2\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = 0
$$

Which can then be simplified down into

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$


::: {.callout-important}
## This is our normal equation
:::

## Estimating $\boldsymbol{\beta}$

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$

To get a formula for estimating $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ we can multiply both
sides of our equation by the inverse of $\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}$
such that

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$


::: {.callout-important}
## The formula requires $\mathbf X$ to have full column rank

This means no column is an exact linear combination of the others
:::

## What if the matrix is not invertible?

If the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are linearly dependent, then
$\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}$ is singular and the usual inverse formula
does not apply

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

- A predictor is an exact linear combination of other predictors
- Two columns are identical
- A categorical variable is represented by all category indicators alongside
  an intercept

Near-linear dependence can also make coefficient estimates numerically
unstable
:::

## A small example

```{r}
#| label: small-data-plot
small_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme_st303()
```

## A small example {style="font-size: 80%;"}

$$
Y = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \qquad
X = \begin{bmatrix} 1  & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$


::: {.fragment}

$$
\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix} \qquad
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23\end{bmatrix}
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\beta_0} \\ \hat{\beta_1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23\end{bmatrix}
$$


$$
\hat{y} = 0.33 + 1.5x
$$

:::

## Representing our variance {style="font-size:80%;"}

### The covariance matrix

Under the model assumptions

$$
E(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=\boldsymbol\beta
$$

Its covariance matrix is

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\widehat{\sigma}^2
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
}
$$

$$
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\sum^n_{i = 1}e^2_i}{n - p}
$$

- The diagonal entries give the estimated variances of the individual
  coefficient estimates
- Taking square roots gives their standard errors
- The off-diagonal entries describe covariances between coefficient
  estimates

## Making predictions from a model

$$
\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta_0} + \hat{\beta_1}x_{i1} + \dots + \hat{\beta_k}x_{ik}
$$

Or in matrix form as

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y} = \mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
$$


:::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Hence for any new configuration of predictors, the predicted conditional mean
becomes

$$
\boxed{\widehat{y_0} = \mathbf{x_0}^\mathsf{T} \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
$$


::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
The row vector $\mathbf x_0^\mathsf T$ must contain the same model terms, in the same order, as the columns of $\mathbf X$
:::
::::

## Constructing confidence intervals

Let's suppose we want to estimate $\mu = \mathcal{E}[y]$ at a particular
value of $\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, x_{01}, x_{02}, \dots x_{0k})^\top$

Our estimate is

$$
\mu_0 = E(Y_0 \mid \mathbf x_0) = \mathbf x_0^\mathsf T \hat{\boldsymbol \beta}
$$

with a standard error of

$$
SE_{\text{fit}}=
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{
\mathbf x_0^\mathsf T
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf x_0
}
$$

A $100 (1 - \alpha)\%$ confidence interval is

$$
\boxed{\widehat y_0 \pm t_{n-p,\,1-\alpha/2}SE_{\text{fit}}}
$$

This interval quantifies uncertainty about the conditional mean response at
the specified predictor values

## Constructing prediction intervals

For a new observation: $\mathbf{x}_0 = (1, x_{01}, x_{02}, ..., x_{0k})^T$,
the estimate is:

$$
\hat{y_0} = \mathbf x_0^\mathsf T \hat{\boldsymbol \beta}
$$

with a predicted standard error

$$
SE_{\text{pred}}=
\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{
1+
\mathbf x_0^\mathsf T
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf x_0
}
$$

Thus, a $100 (1 - \alpha)\%$ prediction interval is

$$
\boxed{\widehat y_0 \pm t_{n-p,\,1-\alpha/2}SE_{\text{pred}}}
$$

## Simple linear regression (using matrices)

Consider the simple linear regression model

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_i + \varepsilon_i
$$

The design matrix can be written as

$$
\mathbf X= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & X_1 \\ 1 & X_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_n \end{bmatrix}
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

The ordinary least squares estimator is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
$$


:::

## Simple linear regression (using matrices) {style="font-size: 70%;"}


::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\mathbf X= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & X_1 \\ 1 & X_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_n \end{bmatrix}
$$

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}

<br>

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ X_1 & X_2 & \cdots & X_n \end{bmatrix}
$$

::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}


::: {.fragment}

<br>

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X= \begin{bmatrix}
n & \sum X_i \\
\sum X_i & \sum X_i^2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::
::::
:::::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix

$$
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1} =
\frac{1}{\text{det}(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)} \begin{bmatrix}
\sum X_i^2 & -\sum X_i \\
-\sum X_i & n
\end{bmatrix} \qquad \text{ where det}(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X) = n\sum X_i^2-\left(\sum X_i\right)^2 = nS_{xx}
$$

:::


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sum Y_i\\
\sum X_iY_i
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::



::::: {.fragment .fade-up}

Multiplying the matrices and simplifying gives

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\boxed{\widehat\beta_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
\boxed{\widehat\beta_0 = \bar Y - \widehat \beta_1 \bar X}
$$

:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Matrix notation generalises the least-squares procedure
:::

:::::

## The coefficient covariance matrix in simple linear regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

Recall that


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

$$
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1} =
\frac{1}{\text{det}(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)} \begin{bmatrix}
\sum X_i^2 & -\sum X_i \\[4pt]
-\sum X_i & n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::
::::

Thus

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2 \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\sum X_i^2}{nS_{xx}} & - \frac{\sum X_i}{nS_{xx}} \\[4pt]
-\frac{\sum X_i}{nS_{xx}} & \frac{n}{nS_{xx}}
\end{bmatrix}
$$


::::: {.fragment .fade-up}


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_0)
=\sigma^2\left(
\frac1n+\frac{\bar X^2}{S_{xx}}
\right)
$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_1)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta_1)
=-\frac{\bar X\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}
$$

:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
The matrix expression gives the variances and covariance of the two coefficient estimates in one calculation.
:::

:::::

## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

Suppose we observe six responses and two predictors

We want to fit

$$
Y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \beta_2X_{i1}^2 + \beta_3X_{i2} +\varepsilon_i
$$


```{r}
#| label: matrix-data

toy_data |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```


## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Constructing the design matrix

The columns must correspond to the model terms in the order

$$
(1,\ X_1,\ X_1^2,\ X_2)
$$

```{r}
#| label: design-matrix
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

X <- model.matrix(~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2, data = toy_data)

X
```

## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Calculate the OLS estimates

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
}
$$

```{r}
#| label: estimate-coefficients
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

# Create the response vector
Y <- matrix(y, ncol = 1)

# Calculate XtX
XtX <- crossprod(X)

# Calculate XtY
XtY <- crossprod(X, Y)

# Calcuate the OLS estimates for the betas
beta_hats <- solve(XtX, XtY)

beta_hats
```


## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### Verifying our answers

```{r}
#| label: verify-model
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + I(x1^2) + x2, data = toy_data)

summary(fit)
```


## Manual matrix calculations in R {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Calculate fitted values and residuals

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

[**Fitted values**]{.center}

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y} = \mathbf X \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

[**Residuals**]{.center}

$$
\mathbf e=\mathbf Y-\widehat{\mathbf Y}
$$

:::
::::

```{r}
#| label: fitted-residuals
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

y_hat <- X %*% beta_hats
e <- Y - y_hat

tibble(
  observed = y,
  fitted = drop(y_hat),
  residual = drop(e)
)
```

## Summary {style="font-size: 75%;"}

The multiple regression model can be expressed as

$$
\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+
\boldsymbol\varepsilon
$$

The OLS estimator is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf Y
$$

when $\mathbf X$ has full column rank

The residuals satisfy

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf e= 0
$$

The estimated coefficient covariance matrix is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\widehat\sigma^2
(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}
$$

These expressions underpin coefficient estimation, uncertainty quantification,
confidence intervals and prediction intervals.
